In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of a prognostically relevant protein biomarker panel for non-small cell lung carcinoma.
the development and validation of a prognostication model based on a protein biomarker panel for surgically resection non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLC) patients.
the question of whether a panel of protein biomarkers can improve survival prediction in patients with non-small cell lung carcinoma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
immunohistochemistry of the biomarkers tested here does not add value to the prognostic information provided by the standard clinicopathological parameters.
the biomarker panel we selected did not outperform the clinical parameters.
the biomarker panel is not superior to the clinical model and that the clinical model is not superior to a biomarker panel.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a panel of protein biomarkers is not superior to clinical parameters in predicting survival of patients with non-small cell lung carcinoma.
the best-performing model based on a panel of five biomarkers did not improve the prediction of overall survival in a cohort of patients with non-small cell lung cancers.
a panel of five biomarkers, MKI67, EZHZ, SLC2a1, CADM, and NKX-2.1 (TTF1), did not improve the prognostication of patients with non-small cell lung carcinoma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should be cautious when introducing new biomarkers into routine clinical care.
we need to be careful when interpreting the results of biomarker studies.

the combination of a prognosic biomarker panel, including MKI67, EZHZ, SLC2AI, CADM1 and NKX2-I, with clinicopathological features does not improve survival prediction over clinical parameters alone in non-small cell cancer.
